item.title: [roundtable.io] How White Sox Turned ‘Organized Chaos’ Into a Postseason Weapon
item.dc:creator: Sam Phalen
item.description: Chicago's unconventional pitching plan has dominated October, but its postseason success was built through a full season of preparation. item.content:encoded:
Chicago's unconventional pitching plan has dominated October, but its postseason success was built through a full season of preparation.
Now just one win away from advancing to the ALCS, it's becoming undeniable that this group has a little bit of magic to it. These White Sox are young, hungry, and they don't know what they don't know.
They show up to the ballpark every day believing they can win. And sometimes in the postseason, that spirit is enough to carry a team.
Baseball, however, isn't just watching Chicago with admiration for the Cinderella story at hand. There's also a somewhat unprecedented strategy being deployed by the White Sox this October, one that could change the way teams shape their pitching staffs moving forward if this level of success continues.
Organized chaos.
That's what the White Sox call their pitching strategy for the postseason.
Right-hander Sean Burke is the only truly reliable traditional starting pitcher the White Sox have on their playoff roster. So Chicago has largely thrown standard pitching roles out the window. Manager Will Venable plays the matchups on a nearly pitch-by-pitch basis, deploying an all-hands-on-deck approach to cover the 27 outs necessary for victory.
Unconventional? Absolutely. But it's also been remarkably effective.
Even Burke hasn't been used as a traditional starting pitcher. And why would he be?
Burke entered Monday's ALDS Game 2 against the Cleveland Guardians in the third inning after Chicago used two openers to begin the game. The White Sox wanted to roll out a pair of left-handers, Anthony Kay and Sean Newcomb, to navigate the top of Cleveland's lineup and neutralize its dangerous left-handed bats before turning things over to Burke.
The strategy also shortened the game for Burke, allowing him to attack hitters without worrying about pacing himself for a traditional six- or seven-inning start.
He was lights out.
Burke pitched into the bottom of the eighth inning and likely could have kept going. At one point, he set a franchise postseason record with 13 consecutive batters retired. Then with the White Sox nursing a 4-2 lead, Venable ultimately decided there was no reason to push it.
The White Sox have now allowed just nine total runs over four postseason games while pitching to a 1.75 team ERA.
All anybody wants to know is how they've managed to make it work. After all, it's not like the White Sox had an incredible pitching staff throughout the regular season. Their 4.12 team ERA was right around the MLB average.
Not to mention, this is an incredibly young White Sox team with plenty of young arms. Many of them are getting their first taste of playoff baseball during this current run. And inexperienced pitchers are usually expected to show some signs of fatigue this late in the season as they blow past previous career highs in innings pitched.
Instead, the opposite has happened. The deeper the White Sox have gotten into the season, the more dominant their pitching staff has become.
So why is it working for Chicago?
Because the White Sox put it into practice during the regular season.
Consistency has been a primary focus for Venable as he takes this young team into the postseason. He wants players in the same positions, doing things they're familiar with. His message in pregame speeches hasn't changed. And when it comes to the pitching staff, they're comfortable being used as Swiss Army knives because that's how they've been deployed all year.
Instead, Chicago learned how to survive without one.
Using an opener in front of a starting pitcher, throwing a bullpen game, asking relievers to cover multiple innings. These are all things the White Sox did during the regular season to get themselves into the playoffs.
Nothing about what Venable is asking his pitchers to do in October is foreign to them. The stakes are higher and the margin for error is smaller, but the roles themselves haven't suddenly changed.
"Organized chaos" from the pitching staff was a necessity for the White Sox to survive 162 games. Now it's becoming a weapon in the postseason.
The young right-hander admitted Chicago's original plan for the game went a bit haywire after Cleveland scored two runs in the first inning, forcing Venable to make an earlier-than-expected move to the bullpen for Newcomb.
But Burke was prepared for the unconventional situation, in part because he leaned on teammates who had already experienced similar roles.
He specifically mentioned Erick Fedde, Sean Newcomb and White Sox bullpen coach Matt Wise as people he leaned on while establishing a routine and rhythm for entering a game after it had already started.
It's another example of why Chicago's organized chaos works. The White Sox aren't improvising in October. They're leaning on the versatility, preparation and experience they spent an entire season developing. Keeping things consistent is an underrated aspect of playoff baseball.
For many teams, the bright lights of October make them tighten up. There's a misconception that you need to play differently and treat these games differently simply because they mean more.
And yes, fundamentally sound baseball becomes increasingly important when the margin for error shrinks. But the White Sox are showing how familiarity, comfort and playing loose can actually be the key to postseason success.
That includes the unconventional approach to team pitching.
It doesn't matter if you're a starter or reliever. It doesn't matter if you're being asked to pitch five innings or throw five pitches. The goal is the same: Get 27 outs.
Guys like Burke are flexible enough to make it work. Venable has continued pushing all the right buttons. And the White Sox have built a pitching staff that's comfortable operating without the traditional roles that have defined the sport for generations.
It started as a necessity during the regular season. It's become one of Chicago's greatest strengths in October.
And if this White Sox playoff run continues, don't be surprised if more teams around Major League Baseball start trying to replicate it.

item.content:encoded:
La postemporada de las Grandes Ligas (MLB) ha alcanzado su punto más candente dentro de la Serie Divisional de la Liga Americana (ALDS). Los Tampa Bay Rays y los New York Yankees se preparan para disputar un crucial Juego 3 que puede definir el destino de ambos conjuntos en su camino hacia la Serie de Campeonato.
En medio de esta encarnizada rivalidad divisional, los reflectores del béisbol mexicano están fijos en la figura de Jonathan Aranda, infielder tijuanense de Tampa Bay que se ha consolidado como un bateador zurdo de enorme impacto y una de las piezas ofensivas clave para la novena de la Florida en octubre.
El escenario de la serie y el rol del mexicano Jonathan Aranda
Tras unos primeros compromisos llenos de intensidad defensiva, sólido pitcheo y jugadas de alto voltaje en Tropicana Field, la eliminatoria traslada sus emociones a la mítica “Catedral del Béisbol” en el Bronx. Tampa Bay ha demostrado tener las armas para plantarle cara a la pesada artillería neoyorquina, destacando el aporte de Aranda en la parte alta y media del orden al bate.
Jonathan Aranda ha vivido una campaña consagratoria. El bateador azteca no solo ha demostrado disciplina en el plato ante los lanzadores de élite de la Gran Carpa, sino que ya sabe lo que es dar cuadrangulares oportunos en instancias de playoffs. Su capacidad para conectar batazos hacia la banda contraria y responder con hombres en posición de anotar lo posiciona como un peligro latente para el cuerpo de pitcheo de Nueva York.
Para este tercer duelo, la presencia de Aranda en la alineación titular de los Rays resultará fundamental para romper el ritmo de los serpentineros rivales y mantener vivas las aspiraciones de su equipo de avanzar a la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Americana (ALCS).
Max Fried contra Nick Martinez: un duelo de pitcheo de alto calibre en el Bronx
De cara a este vital compromiso, la directiva de los Yankees, encabezada por el mánager Aaron Boone, ha confirmado a su abridor estrella: el zurdo Max Fried. El experimentado serpentinero saltará a la lomita del Yankee Stadium con la responsabilidad de frenar a la ofensiva de Tampa Bay y consolidar la ventaja neoyorquina.
Fried llega a este encuentro con la confianza en lo más alto tras una salida brillante en la Serie de Wild Card frente a los Red Sox de Boston, donde lanzó 6 entradas permitiendo solo una carrera limpia y recetando seis ponches. Además, el zurdo ostenta antecedentes dominantes ante los Rays, registrando una efectividad histórica de 1.26 en sus enfrentamientos directos contra la franquicia de Florida.
Por parte de los Tampa Bay Rays, el encargado de subirse al montículo será el derecho Nick Martinez, quien firmó una temporada regular brillante con foja de 15-6 y una efectividad de 3.10 en 31 aperturas. Martinez realizará la primera apertura de postemporada de su carrera en Las Mayores, en un entorno de máxima exigencia como lo es el Bronx.
- Equipo: Tampa Bay Rays
- Récord en Temporada Regular: 15-6
- Efectividad (ERA): 3.10
- WHIP: 1.09
En caso de que la serie se extienda, Aaron Boone ya tiene proyectado al zurdo Carlos Rodón para el Juego 4, contando además con la opción de disponer del estelar Gerrit Cole desde el bullpen si la situación así lo requiere.
¿Dónde ver en vivo el partido desde México?
- Partido: Tampa Bay Rays vs. New York Yankees (Juego 3 de la Serie Divisional de la Liga Americana)
- Fecha: Miércoles 7 de octubre de 2026
- Horario en México: 18:00 horas (Tiempo del Centro de México, CST) / 20:00 horas (Tiempo del Este de EE. UU., ET)
- Estadio: Yankee Stadium, El Bronx, Nueva York
Los aficionados al béisbol en territorio mexicano podrán seguir cada turno al bate de Jonathan Aranda y la transmisión completa del Juego 3 a través de televisión restringida y servicios de streaming:
- Televisión de Paga: ESPN y Fox Sports (señales disponibles en los principales sistemas de TV por cable e izzi/Sky).
- Streaming en vivo: Disney+ (Suscripción Premium), MLB.TV (Suscripción Pass de Postemporada) y Prime Video (vía canal Fox Sports/ESPN).

item.content:encoded:
The scenes shift for Game 3 of the National League Division Series on Tuesday, Oct. 6, and prediction markets offer great trading opportunities.
Unpredictable things happen during the MLB postseason, but if you think you know what will happen, you can stake your claim on Kalshi and Polymarket US.
Aces Chris Sale and Yoshinobu Yamamoto will square off at Atlanta’s Truist Park in a star-studded pitching matchup between the Braves and two-time defending champion Los Angeles Dodgers. The series is even at 1 after Atlanta’s 3-2 win at Dodger Stadium in Game 2.
The Milwaukee Brewers will try to sweep the San Diego Padres in the nightcap at San Diego’s Petco Park.
Let’s look closer at the best sports prediction markets and prices for today’s two games.
Best MLB props for National League Playoffs today
LA Dodgers at Atlanta Braves over/under market
Why Over 6.5 runs could hit
Probability: 51% at Kalshi
Sale and Yamamoto are aces, but these are two of baseball’s most prolific offenses. The Dodgers, of course, have MVPs batting Nos. 1-3 (Mookie Betts, Shohei Ohtani and Freddie Freeman), and Freeman is heating up after an ice-cold September.
Seven runs isn’t a high bar to clear, especially considering Sale’s struggles in October. Sale has a 5.83 ERA in 12 career postseason appearances and allowed three runs to the Phillies in his last postseason start.
The teams totaled eight runs in Game 1, which Dodgers star Tarik Skubal started.
Why Under 6.5 runs could hit
Probability: 49% at ProphetX
These are two of the best pitchers in baseball, and Yamamoto specifically has been a big-game pitcher since he came over from Japan. He was the 2025 World Series MVP. Fewer than seven runs were scored in five of his nine career postseason starts.
Sale has been a bulldog throughout his career, and he’ll need to rise to the occasion to match Yamamoto in an enormous game.
Even though these offenses have elite players, they have not gotten unlocked. Braves star outfielder Ronald Acuna Jr. has a .485 postseason OPS, and Matt Olsen’s is .543. On the Dodgers’ side, Ohtani, Betts and Will Smith have combined for three hits in 21 at-bats.
Those numbers don’t bode well when facing aces. The first team to two runs may win Game 3.
Milwaukee Brewers at San Diego Padres first five innings market
Why the Padres could win the first five innings
Probability: 47% at Polymarket
The Padres have been striking early throughout the postseason. They have scored first in all four games and have held 2-0 leads in each game in this series.
The Padres have been one of the most dominant teams at home this year, too. They went 51-30 at Petco Park during the regular season and had no trouble rolling the Cubs in the Wild Card round.
Plus, Dustin May is by far the Brewers’ shakiest starting pitcher. He has good career numbers against the Padres (3.14 ERA in 86 innings) but also may be nervous since this will be his first postseason appearance in six years.
Why the Brewers could win the first five innings
Probability: 37% at Kalshi
Milwaukee’s offense has been slow to get going in the series, but it can keep the momentum after its emotional win over the Padres and closer Mason Miller in Game 2.
May may not get more than three innings, but the Brewers bullpen has been awesome, especially in this series. Milwaukee has not allowed any runs in nine innings.
If May can hold down San Diego for one turn through the order, the Brewers can win the first five innings and Game 3.
How prediction markets work for MLB Playoffs trading
All prediction market trades are peer-to-peer, meaning you need a fellow user to buy and sell shares.
Users buy ‘Yes’ and ‘No’ shares on sports results. Each share costs $0.01 to $0.99. All winning shares pay out $1. Losing shares pay out nothing. Low share prices produce bigger payouts.
You can use prediction markets like a sportsbook and wait for your game to finish, or you can use them like the registered financial exchanges they are. If you choose the latter, you can day trade outcomes by buying shares at a low price and selling higher for incremental profit.
Of course, there is risk with any way you trade on sports. Luckily, you can earn valuable site credit by claiming new-user bonuses with the top prediction market promos.

item.content:encoded:
MLB Best Bets Today October 6
The AL steps aside and the NL takes center stage, as we get Game 3s with a change of scenery in Dodgers vs. Braves and Brewers vs. Padres. After a long day of travel, the teams are back at it, as San Diego looks to stave off elimination and LA and Atlanta are both searching for a huge win to take control of the series. That game has Yoshinobu Yamamoto vs. Chris Sale, while the other game has the potential for all kinds of craziness and lots of bullpen arms. Two very different games to say the least.
Throughout the playoffs, I’ll look at every game on the schedule, even if I don’t have any bets. I’ll typically do this on the morning of the games, trying to achieve as much lead time as possible. Bullpen usage is critically important in the postseason, so I’d be doing a major disservice to do anything before the games are finished and that usually means writing up my thoughts in the morning.
All lines are from DraftKings and are current at the time of publish. Please take the initiative to SHOP AROUND for the best odds. It matters. A lot.
One offering this baseball season is our Opta AI Player Prop Projections. They are for VSiN Pro Subscribers only, so you can check out our current offers here.
Feel free to use my opinions and thoughts, as well as our suite of MLB Betting Tools, including the DraftKings and Circa Betting Splits, Steve Makinen’s Daily Ratings, the 1st 5 Innings Analyzer, and Umpire Stats.
Here are the MLB best bets today for October 6:
Dodgers vs. Braves (-110, 6)
6 p.m. ET
The Dodgers and Braves have flipped back and forth as ever so slight favorites in what is basically a coin-flip affair in Atlanta. The total of 6 definitely illustrates the quality of this pitching matchup, especially because of the caliber of the players in these two lineups. Obviously the Dodgers were among the league’s best and the Braves, while very talented, had a lot of inconsistencies with their hitters.
Sale finished the regular season with a 2.16 ERA, 2.97 xERA, and a 2.29 FIP over his 162.2 innings of work. So far this postseason, he’s pitched 7.2 innings with one start and one relief effort, allowing three runs on five hits with a 12/2 K/BB ratio. Some will probably point to his poor postseason numbers with a 5.83 ERA over 41.2 innings of work, but this is his first time back in the playoffs since 2021, so I’m not really sure any of that matters for what he is now.
LA was fifth in wOBA at .331 against LHP during the regular season, though not all lefties are created equal and not many are Sale. If we start cutting down the sample size, the Dodgers were seventh in wOBA at .329 in the second half against lefties and second with a .366 wOBA in the month of September. But, their 13% BB% is not applicable against a guy like Sale, who throws a lot of strikes.
I’m a bit surprised that the Dodgers didn’t roll with Yamamoto in Game 2, opting instead for Blake Snell. Yamamoto had a 2.53 ERA with a 2.94 xERA and a 3.33 FIP during the regular season over 185 innings. He also would have broken up the run of two straight lefties, but Dave Roberts acknowledged that the Dodgers were thinking about their rotation with the NLCS already, which is pretty presumptuous and was probably some bulletin board material for the Braves.
Yamamoto has already thrown 56 postseason innings with a 2.25 ERA and a 3.45 FIP, as his K% hasn’t been as high, but his BB% has been even better. The Braves were 11th in the league with a .319 wOBA against righties. They were definitely worse against lefties, which perhaps had something to do with Snell being the Game 2 call. The Braves had .316 wOBA against RHP in the second half and had a .317 wOBA against them in September.
Sale has only allowed more than three runs in one start this season, which happened back on April 6. Yamamoto allowed four runs in two of his four September starts. This is a very tight game to say the least. I don’t like a pregame bet in this one. I don’t even have a line on side or total.
Brewers vs. Padres (-138, 7.5)
9:30 p.m. ET
Dustin May and Nick Pivetta are the listed starters here, as this is a much different game than the other one. I’m actually not expecting to see May for very long. I think the right-hander is going to get the team through Fernando Tatis, Manny Machado, and Ty France at least once and maybe try to navigate the bottom of the lineup. My expectation is that we see both Robert Gasser and Shane Drohan. Maybe even Kyle Harrison. There is a lot of data out there about teams hitting relievers better the more that they see them. Those three and Chad Patrick have not pitched yet in this series.
Meanwhile, Trevor Megill, Abner Uribe, and Aaron Ashby have all pitched in both games, while Antonio Senzatela, JoJo Romero, and DL Hall each have one appearance. This will be an all hands on deck approach from Milwaukee and I wouldn’t be surprised if the Padres hitters see a different arm in each plate appearance. May in a short burst sitting 98-99 with movement might fare a bit better than what he usually does.
On the San Diego side, Pivetta really struggled his way through 3.1 innings against the Cubs with four strikeouts and two walks. He only gave up one run on three hits, but it was an arduous appearance. Pivetta only made eight starts during the regular season, with four to start the season and four to finish it. He only allowed 11 runs over 34.2 innings when all was said and done and just three runs in his final four starts.
Joe Musgrove and David Morgan have not pitched in this series yet. Yuki Matsui and Bradgley Rodriguez worked back-to-back days in Games 1 and 2. Mason Miller threw 40 pitches with the loss in Game 2 and Adrian Morejon threw 31 with the loss in Game 1. We could see Walker Buehler here as well as Robbie Ray.
I like the setup better for Milwaukee here with a cavalcade of arms, including several lefties that they can deploy if they wish. I don’t think May will factor into the game as much as the line implies. More specialists for Milwaukee can pitch in the middle innings and guys who can give the Friars a different look. As the underdog price, I think the Brewers are worth a look tonight.
Pick: Brewers +114

item.dc:creator: Ben Clemens

item.content:encoded:
When I’m trying to ground myself in the present, I like to repeat a mantra: No past, no future. I don’t want to dictate personal philosophy to you, but it works great for me. It’s a reminder to focus on the now, that experiencing what’s happening right this instant is more important than whatever mental baggage I’m carrying or whatever I’m worried might take place next week. I wholeheartedly suggest some variation of this phrase when you’re feeling overwhelmed by things that aren’t happening to you in the moment.
Having said that, let me be clear: You can’t ignore the past and future when you’re managing postseason pitching assignments, Walt Weiss. The Braves are five games into the playoffs, and they’ve been living the “no past, no future” life the entire time. Now, I actually think that has some useful consequences. The present really does matter quite a bit in playoff baseball – more than the future, and certainly more than the past. But it’s also caused them plenty of problems. The clearest example is also the most notable move Weiss has made so far. The Braves deployed bullpen games in each of the first two games of the NLDS over the weekend. The first was unavoidable, a consequence of their injury-depleted rotation, but the second was the direct consequence of Weiss’ earlier actions.
I’m talking about Chris Sale, of course. Sale started the Wild Card opener against the Phillies last Tuesday and worked into the seventh, throwing 95 pitches before departing with two on, one out, and the bottom of the Philly lineup coming to the plate. After a little turbulence (Didier Fuentes allowed both inherited runners to score, giving the Phillies the lead), the Braves pulled it out. But after Philadelphia won the second game of the series, Weiss called on Sale to cover the final four outs of the decisive Game 3.
Ben is a writer at FanGraphs. He can be found on Bluesky @benclemens.

item.content:encoded:
The 2026 MLB postseason continues Monday with Game 2 of both American League Division Series. The Chicago White Sox continued their perfect start to the playoffs, winning again over the Cleveland Guardians to take a 2-0 series lead. The White Sox are now 4-0 in the postseason, with all four victories coming on the road.
The New York Yankees, meanwhile, are trying to even their series against the Tampa Bay Rays behind Cy Young favorite Cam Schlittler.
Since the best-of-five Division Series became a thing in 1995, the team that won Game 1 has gone on to win the series 73% of the time, and 32% of the time the series ended in a sweep. Winning Game 1 doesn't guarantee a series win, but the White Sox and Rays are in the driver's seat at the moment. Here are the final scores and schedule for Monday's playoff action:
- FINAL: White Sox 4, Guardians 3 (box score); White Sox lead series 2-0
- LIVE: Yankees at Rays (GameTracker); Rays lead series 1-0
To sum up all the ALDS Game 2 action, we're here to declare a winner and loser from both games. You can find those authoritative and inarguable declarations just below.
Winner: The Garrett Crochet trade
For the second time this postseason, the three position players the White Sox received in the Garrett Crochet trade with the Red Sox guided them to a win. , and in Game 2 of the ALDS on Monday. Those three players -- Chase Meidroth, Braden Montgomery, Kyle Teel -- went a combined 4 for 12 with 3 RBI.
Teel helped the White Sox get on the board with his leadoff single in the fourth inning. He later came around to score Chicago's first run on a Munetaka Murakami single. Montgomery provided the game's biggest blow. He drove a two-out, two-run double to right field in the sixth inning, which flipped a 2-1 deficit into a 3-2 lead for the White Sox. This, as the kids say, is a nice piece of hitting:
Meidroth followed with a single to right to score Montgomery and give the White Sox what proved to be an important insurance run. The Crochet trade bounty had four of Chicago's six hits in Game 2 and either scored or drove in all four runs. Sean Burke, who was not part of the Crochet trade, threw 5 ⅓ innings of one-run ball behind a pair of openers. He struck out six. He was terrific.
The White Sox did not want to trade Crochet two years ago. They'd just lost a modern record 121 games, however, and needed to add talent up and down the roster. So, Crochet was dealt to Boston, and it sure seems like GM Chris Getz nailed the trade. Three of the four players he received in the deal are playing major roles in October. This is how you draw it up.
are now one win away from their first ALCS since their 2005 World Series win.
Loser: GuardsBall
It is really, really hard to hit in the postseason. Don't believe me? Teams came into Monday hitting .211/.293/.352 this postseason, and .174/.277/.295 in the Division Series. The pitchers are so nasty, they're well-rested thanks to the built-in off-days, and their matchups are all optimized. Every base hit in the postseason is a tiny little miracle, I swear.
The Guardians, two games into their postseason run, are learning that the hard way. They were shut out in Game 1 and held to three hits. In Game 2, they had only four hits, three of which were singles. To date, Cleveland's biggest offensive play in the ALDS is Sean Newcomb's two-run throwing error in the first inning Monday. Here are two of the three runs the Guardians scored in Game 2 (and in the series):
Including Newcomb's error, four of the first five Guardians reached base in Game 2. Only four of the final 30 reached base, most notably Jo Adell's RBI triple in the eighth inning. With all due respect, this is not a dominant White Sox pitching staff. They've had to cobble it together with openers and bullpen games this postseason. Credit to them for keeping Cleveland in check.
The Guardians are not exactly an offensive powerhouse though. They ranked 24th in runs and 27th in home runs during the regular season. It's the same story every year. The Guardians rally in the second half to win the AL Central, then have a hard time putting points on the board in October. That is certainly the case this year. Three runs on seven hits through two ALDS games. Yeesh.
Cleveland is one loss away from elimination. The Guardians are 2-8 in their last 10 postseason games dating back to 2024.

item.content:encoded:
The Athletic has live coverage of the MLB Playoffs, including the ALDS Game 2s of White Sox vs Guardians and Yankees vs Rays.
After three days of Wild Card Series action, the dust has settled and four teams (Houston Astros, Boston Red Sox, Philadelphia Phillies and Chicago Cubs) have found themselves on an early vacation. Major League Baseball’s 12-team postseason field has been whittled to eight.
Now, the race for the World Series shifts to the next round: the Division Series. Four teams (Cleveland Guardians, Los Angeles Dodgers, Tampa Bay Rays and Milwaukee Brewers) that had first-round byes will now be in action. Additionally, while the Wild Card Series featured a best-of-three format, the Division Series will be best-of-five.
Here’s how MLB’s bracket looks right now:
You can watch the MLB playoffs on Fubo (Stream Free Now).
What is Saturday’s MLB Playoff schedule and starters?
White Sox at Guardians (AL Division Series Game 1): Hagen Smith vs. Parker Messick
First pitch: 1 p.m. ET (TBS)
After the 23-year-old Smith pitched three scoreless innings in Game 1 of the Wild Card Series against the Astros, the White Sox turn to him for an encore performance in Game 1 of the ALDS. While the club was able to pile on six runs against the Astros in a win, it won’t be as easy against the Guardians and Messick.
An All-Star this season, Messick finished his rookie campaign with a 2.56 ERA and 193 strikeouts over 32 starts. Against the White Sox, Messick carded a 2.81 ERA in four starts (25 2/3 innings).
Braves at Dodgers (NL Division Series Game 1): TBD vs. Tarik Skubal
First pitch: 4 p.m. ET (Fox)
Having burned Chris Sale to take Thursday’s winner-take-all game against the Phillies, and with Tyler Mahle also unavailable, the Braves appear to be looking at another bullpen game.
“They’ve pitched in big situations during the season, and no matter who we really see right now in that bullpen in any situation, no matter what inning it is, we’re feeling pretty confident about them,” catcher Drake Baldwin told reporters.
The Dodgers, coming off a first-round bye, will counter with Tarik Skubal, the crown jewel acquisition of this year’s trade deadline. The AL’s reigning Cy Young Award winner has a 2.61 ERA with his new team, his final starts before reaching a highly anticipated free agency.
Yankees at Rays (AL Division Series Game 1): Gerrit Cole vs. Drew Rasmussen
First pitch: 6:30 p.m. ET (TBS)
Faced with an embarrassment of riches on the pitching side, the Yankees will deploy 2023 AL Cy Young Award winner Gerrit Cole against the AL East champs. After Cole in Game 1, the Yankees will have Cam Schlittler in Game 2 and some variation of Max Fried or Carlos Rodón in Games 3 and 4, the last matchup only if necessary.
On the Tampa Bay side, Drew Rasmussen, arguably one of the most underrated aces in the sport, will get the ball at Tropicana Field. For his career, Rasmussen has a 1.81 ERA in 11 games (10 starts) against the Yankees.
Padres at Brewers (NL Division Series Game 1): Robbie Ray vs. Jacob Misiorowski
First pitch: 8:30 p.m. ET (FS1)
Saturday’s final matchup will feature two pitchers at opposite ends of their careers. On the San Diego side, Robbie Ray, the 2021 AL Cy Young Award winner, has been largely unable to replicate the success he had that season. After a deadline trade from the San Francisco Giants to the Padres, Ray has carded a 5.02 ERA over nine starts.
For the Brewers, Jacob Misiorowski is just getting started. An All-Star in his rookie year, Misiorowski finished his sophomore campaign as the favorite to win the NL Cy Young Award, leading MLB with a 1.80 ERA and 252 strikeouts. He’s wowed the sport with his ability to repeatedly fire fastballs in excess of 100 mph, and there’s reason to believe that, at 24 years old, his best is yet to come.
What to know about each Division Series matchup
White Sox at Guardians: The two AL Central clubs played each other 13 times during the regular season, with the White Sox winning the season series 7-6. That, however, was not enough to overcome a late surge by the Guardians and a collapse by Chicago that led to the White Sox losing control of the division and having to play their way out of the wild card.
Now, the two clubs will meet again for at least three games, a spot in the Championship Series on the line. By winning the division and finishing with a better record than the AL West winner, the Guardians were granted a first-round bye. No mind, the White Sox dispatched the Astros in two games and have been off since Thursday. That extra rest has allowed the club to realign its depleted pitching staff.
One thing to watch: How Chicago’s thin, matchup-dependent pitching staff is deployed against Cleveland’s newfound offense — the club led the AL in wRC+ (108) from Aug. 1 onward. The urgency, or lack thereof, by White Sox manager Will Venable could swing the series either direction.
Braves at Dodgers: The Braves’ pitching staff will enter Game 1 with very little margin for error, as it will likely be a group effort without a starter available. That alone could be the difference, as teams that take Game 1 in any best-of-five series have historically won the series 72 percent of the time. That said, these Dodgers have not played their best against the Braves, losing the season series 5-1, including a late-August sweep when Tyler Glasnow and Yoshinobu Yamamoto both pitched.
One thing to watch: Shohei Ohtani’s ability to contribute. The four-time MVP has spent much of the second half of the season compromised, leading to an abbreviated September, with some of it on the injured list.
“I do feel like my swing is in a better place, feels smooth, and just a little tweaks here and there, and I’ll be ready for tomorrow,” Ohtani said through interpreter Will Ireton.
Yankees at Rays: Only one team had a better record over its final 30 games than the Rays, who went 20-10 to fend off a late Yankees push to claim the AL East. That, plus a 55-26 home record that tied the Brewers for the best in MLB, has Tampa Bay inching toward its first World Series appearance since 2020. To get there, the Rays will need to beat the Yankees, who made quick work of the Red Sox in the wild-card round. That they did so without Aaron Judge on the roster or needing to call on Giancarlo Stanton in a pinch hit capacity is all the more impressive.
One thing to watch: Junior Caminero was 20 years old the last time the Rays made the postseason, going hitless in two at-bats. Since then, Caminero, now 23, has morphed into a perennial All-Star, hitting 40 home runs in consecutive seasons, the latter of which should earn him major MVP consideration. Few players love the big stage as much as Caminero. One of those players just so happens to be Cam Schlittler, the presumptive AL Cy Young Award winner, who will take the ball at least once this series. How these two match up will be one of the best subplots of this postseason.
Padres at Brewers: In a battle between arguably MLB’s hottest team (the Padres) and the league’s best team all season (the Brewers), there will be a lot of firsts. This is San Diego’s first Division Series under new owners José E. Feliciano and his wife and business partner Kwanza Jones. It will be the first extended runway for Padres rookie catcher Ethan Salas. It will be the first postseason series for Christian Yelich as the Brewers’ captain. And it will be the first time Misiorowski faces these Padres since May.
Should Milwaukee win, it will be the first time in franchise history that the club has made it to back-to-back league championship series. If San Diego upsets MLB’s No. 1 team, it will be the club’s first trip since 2022 and just its fourth overall.
One thing to watch: The bullpens. Behind multiple high-leverage arms, San Diego has made the late innings nearly impossible for opposing teams. If there’s one club that can match the Padres in that regard, it’s the Brewers. The late innings will likely be the deciding factor in who advances.

item.content:encoded:
Ranking Every MLB Playoff Team's Projected 2026 Postseason Rotation
Pitching wins championships.
While that old adage still holds true, it has taken on a slightly different meaning in today's game, as teams need to successfully utilize their entire pitching staff to make a deep playoff run, rather than simply leaning on two or three starting pitchers to shoulder the load.
Still, a strong performance from the starting staff can give a team a major leg up. The Los Angeles Dodgers were the perfect example of that last October.
Ahead, we've ranked the playoff rotations of every postseason team. Which team's rotation is best positioned heading into the playoffs?
12. Houston Astros
1 of 12
RHP Hunter Brown (6-3, 3.26 ERA, 1.28 WHIP, 120 K, 102.0 IP)
RHP Hayden Wesneski (5-2, 3.50 ERA, 1.15 WHIP, 41 K, 54.0 IP)
RHP Peter Lambert (8-10, 3.87 ERA, 1.26 WHIP, 153 K, 153.2 IP)
RHP Ethan Pecko (1-0, 4.31 ERA, 1.21 WHIP, 21 K, 31.1 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Ronel Blanco, RHP Cristian Javier (out for ALWC)
The Astros have used 19 different starting pitchers this year while navigating a long list of injuries. The fact that reliever AJ Blubaugh ranks third on the team with 95.1 innings pitched speaks volumes.
Ace Hunter Brown was slowed by a shoulder strain in the first half of the season, but he has returned to form with a 3.11 ERA and 81 strikeouts in 66.2 innings since the All-Star break.
With Cristian Javier making an early exit from his start on Wednesday, the rotation behind Brown is entirely up in the air. Hayden Wesneski and Peter Lambert are both capable of tossing a quality start, but they are short on big-game experience and could also be susceptible to a quick hook, shifting the focus to a Houston bullpen that ranks 17th in the majors with a 4.09 ERA.
11. Chicago White Sox
2 of 12
RHP Sean Burke (10-7, 3.40 ERA, 1.20 WHIP, 178 K, 167.0 IP)
RHP Davis Martin (9-7, 3.84 ERA, 1.29 WHIP, 121 K, 145.1 IP)
RHP Erick Fedde (8-9, 3.83 ERA, 1.36 WHIP, 99 K, 141.0 IP)
LHP Anthony Kay (9-9, 4.53 ERA, 1.37 WHIP, 125 K, 153.0 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Luis Castillo, RHP David Sandlin
The White Sox rank 26th in starters' ERA (4.62) and 28th in quality starts (34), so the starting rotation is something they will need to figure out how to navigate in the postseason rather than a strength.
Sean Burke and Davis Martin have accounted for 21 of those 33 quality starts. They will be asked to chew up innings at the top of the rotation, while games outside of their starts will likely be an all-hands-on-deck situation.
Sean Newcomb (58 G, 6 GS, 3.17 ERA, 88.0 IP) and Grant Taylor (59 G, 4 GS, 2.30 ERA, 82.0 IP) are both capable of providing length out of the bullpen, while deadline pickup Luis Castillo has also been shifted to a relief role.
10. Chicago Cubs
3 of 12
LHP Shota Imanaga (11-10, 3.74 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, 171 K, 173.1 IP)
RHP Kevin Gausman (4-2, 4.83 ERA, 1.23 WHIP, 57 K, 50.1 IP)
LHP Matthew Boyd (10-5, 3.91 ERA, 1.21 WHIP, 96 K, 126.2 IP)
LHP David Peterson (6-2, 3.94 ERA, 1.39 WHIP, 68 K, 75.1 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Clay Holmes, RHP Javier Assad
The Cubs roll into October with arguably the best offense and best defense in baseball, but questions about their pitching staff hang over their postseason outlook.
Shota Imanaga has a 1.96 ERA and a 23-to-2 strikeout-to-walk ratio over 23 innings in September. That should put him in line to be the ace of the staff in October.
Veteran Kevin Gausman's significant playoff experience, including starting Game 2 and Game 6 of the World Series a year ago, should earn him a prominent role in the playoffs. At the back of the staff, Clay Holmes is the obvious candidate to shift to the bullpen given his past experience closing games.
9. San Diego Padres
4 of 12
RHP Michael King (12-10, 3.21 ERA, 1.18 WHIP, 159 K, 185.0 IP)
RHP Nick Pivetta (3-2, 2.86 ERA, 1.01 WHIP, 42 K, 34.2 IP)
RHP Walker Buehler (9-6, 4.56 ERA, 1.34 WHIP, 128 K, 150.0 IP)
LHP Robbie Ray (3-2, 5.02 ERA, 1.54 WHIP, 33 K, 43.0 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Casey Mize, RHP Randy Vásquez
The Padres rank fourth in the majors and top among projected playoff teams with 666.0 innings of work from their bullpen. That relief corps, anchored by Mason Miller and Adrian Morejón, will be a major factor in October.
Michael King is the clear ace of the staff. Nick Pivetta has pitched well since returning on Sept. 7, with 11 hits and three earned runs allowed in 14 innings over three starts.
Behind them, Walker Buehler is the logical Game 3 candidate, given his postseason resume and 3.15 ERA over 45.2 innings in his last nine starts. Deadline pickups Robbie Ray and Casey Mize have struggled since coming to San Diego and could be X-factors if they advance beyond the Wild Card Round.
8. Cleveland Guardians
5 of 12
RHP Gavin Williams (14-8, 3.63 ERA, 1.08 WHIP, 244 K, 181.0 IP)
LHP Parker Messick (12-9, 2.55 ERA, 1.04 WHIP, 191 K, 183.1 IP)
RHP Tanner Bibee (6-15, 4.35 ERA, 1.22 WHIP, 142 K, 182.0 IP)
LHP Joey Cantillo (11-9, 3.62 ERA, 1.42 WHIP, 171 K, 159.0 IP)
Other Candidates: LHP Foster Griffin
Gavin Williams leads the AL with 244 strikeouts and Parker Messick has a 2.27 ERA in 71.1 innings since the All-Star break, giving the Guardians a legitimate one-two punch to lead the way in the postseason.
Opening Day starter Tanner Bibee has struggled, posting an 8.24 ERA over 19.2 innings in September, but his track record still makes him the most likely candidate to start Game 3.
The question then becomes who gets the nod between Foster Griffin and Joey Cantillo. Griffin has a 5.19 ERA in nine starts since he was acquired at the trade deadline, while Cantillo has better surface-level results but has issued an AL-leading 81 walks in 159 innings.
7. Atlanta Braves
6 of 12
LHP Chris Sale (14-9, 2.16 ERA, 0.98 WHIP, 200 K, 162.2 IP)
RHP Tyler Mahle (4-1, 1.99 ERA, 0.96 WHIP, 48 K, 54.1 IP)
RHP Grant Holmes (10-5, 3.47 ERA, 1.30 WHIP, 114 K, 147.2 IP)
RHP JR Ritchie (1-4, 4.79 ERA, 1.46 WHIP, 66 K, 67.2 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Bryce Elder, RHP AJ Smith-Shawver, LHP Martín Pérez (out for NLWC)
Starting pitching was expected to be a glaring issue for the Braves when Spencer Strider, Spencer Schwellenbach, Hurston Waldrep and AJ Smith-Shawver all began the season on the injured list.
Instead, Chris Sale has put together a Cy Young-caliber season, while journeyman veterans Martín Pérez and Grant Holmes have combined for a 3.26 ERA in 289.2 innings spanning 55 starts. However, Pérez was just placed on the injured list with lower back inflammation, making a bullpen game the likely approach to fill the fourth starter role if they advance to the NLDS.
Deadline pickup Tyler Mahle has given them the No. 2 starter they still lacked, while a healthy Bryce Elder could be an X-factor if they advance deeper into October.
6. Milwaukee Brewers
7 of 12
RHP Jacob Misiorowski (15-5, 1.86 ERA, 0.80 WHIP, 247 K, 169.1 IP)
RHP Logan Henderson (11-3, 2.47 ERA, 0.84 WHIP, 110 K, 98.1 IP)
LHP Robert Gasser (5-5, 4.01 ERA, 1.24 WHIP, 94 K, 103.1 IP)
RHP Dustin May (2-2, 5.61 ERA, 1.43 WHIP, 33 K, 33.2 IP)
Other Candidates: LHP Kyle Harrison, LHP Shane Drohan
Jacob Misiorowski pitched out of the bullpen for the Brewers last October, posting a 1.50 ERA, 0.83 WHIP and 16 strikeouts in 12 innings across three appearances. He is now poised to lead their staff this postseason.
Rookie Logan Henderson has not allowed more than three earned runs in any of his 18 starts this season. He is 8-2 with a 2.19 ERA and 0.79 WHIP in 70 innings since the All-Star break.
Left-hander Robert Gasser has a 1.71 ERA in 26.1 innings over his last five appearances. He will be a significant part of manager Pat Murphy's plan of mixing and matching innings behind Misiorowski and Henderson.
5. Boston Red Sox
8 of 12
RHP Sonny Gray (18-5, 2.72 ERA, 1.15 WHIP, 149 K, 169.0 IP)
LHP Ranger Suarez (8-5, 3.22 ERA, 1.19 WHIP, 140 K, 148.1 IP)
LHP Payton Tolle (9-6, 3.03 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, 171 K, 148.2 IP)
RHP Brayan Bello (6-7, 4.49 ERA, 1.37 WHIP, 90 K, 112.1 IP)
Other Candidates: LHP Jake Bennett, LHP Patrick Sandoval
Few offseason additions have made a bigger impact than Sonny Gray, who has 20 quality starts in 29 games this year and is on track for his fourth career top-10 finish in Cy Young voting for four different teams.
Rookie Payton Tolle has been the team's most consistent starter behind Gray this year and will factor into the playoff rotation, while high-priced offseason signing Ranger Suarez has a 1.09 ERA over 24.2 innings in September.
The X-factor could be Brayan Bello after he threw a gem (8.0 IP, 5 H, 1 ER, 11 K) on the road against the Rays on Sept. 19. He has a 2.28 ERA over 51.1 innings while working mostly out of the bullpen since returning from a minor league demotion before the All-Star break, but he is stretched back out to start.
4. Tampa Bay Rays
9 of 12
RHP Drew Rasmussen (16-5, 2.67 ERA, 0.91 WHIP, 174 K, 172.0 IP)
RHP Nick Martinez (15-5, 2.94 ERA, 1.07 WHIP, 108 K, 177.1 IP)
RHP Freddy Peralta (4-2, 3.60 ERA, 0.98 WHIP, 39 K, 50.0 IP)
RHP Griffin Jax (8-10, 3.62 ERA, 1.19 WHIP, 115 K, 109.1 IP)
Other Candidates: LHP Ian Seymour, LHP Shane McClanahan (out for ALDS)
Few organizations do a better job fully utilizing the entire pitching staff than the Rays, but this October they have three legitimate rotation anchors who can get them deep into games in Drew Rasmussen, Nick Martinez and deadline pickup Freddy Peralta.
That group gets even deeper if Shane McClanahan returns to action, though he has already been ruled out for the ALDS. Even if he's not able to return, reliever-turned-starter Griffin Jax has also been quietly excellent this season with a 3.23 ERA and 105 strikeouts in 100.1 innings over his 22 starts.
They could still opt to utilize an opener when it makes sense, or piggyback one of their starters with left-hander Ian Seymour if the situation arises. This isn't a staff that needs to lean on multiple bullpen games to get through a series.
3. Philadelphia Phillies
10 of 12
LHP Cristopher Sánchez (18-6, 2.93 ERA, 1.22 WHIP, 221 K, 200.0 IP)
RHP Zack Wheeler (13-5, 3.06 ERA, 1.06 WHIP, 188 K, 156.0 IP)
RHP Aaron Nola (7-11, 4.54 ERA, 1.33 WHIP, 177 K, 174.1 IP)
LHP Jesús Luzardo (14-5, 2.87 ERA, 1.08 WHIP, 221 K, 178.2 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Andrew Painter
Jesús Luzardo played catch earlier this week as he works his way back from shoulder inflammation, though his postseason status remains up in the air. There's a chance he will be limited to bullpen work early in the playoffs.
Veteran Aaron Nola has hit his stride of late, posting a 2.45 ERA in 66 innings over his last 11 starts, so he can fill the void behind the dynamic one-two punch of Cristopher Sánchez (7.7 WAR, 1st among all SP) and Zack Wheeler (5.6 WAR, 8th among all SP).
The Phillies rank second in the majors with 73 quality starts and 869.1 innings from their starting staff, so they are poised to lean on their starters as hard as anyone in October.
2. New York Yankees
11 of 12
RHP Cam Schlittler (14-6, 1.95 ERA, 0.92 WHIP, 239 K, 193.2 IP)
LHP Max Fried (5-5, 2.80 ERA, 0.99 WHIP, 104 K, 112.2 IP)
RHP Gerrit Cole (10-9, 3.61 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, 131 K, 127.0 IP)
LHP Carlos Rodón (7-3, 2.67 ERA, 1.06 WHIP, 91 K, 84.1 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Will Warren
With AL Cy Young favorite Cam Schlittler and three established veteran starters capable of frontline production in Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodón, the Yankees rotation is capable of making a major impact in October.
Schlittler logged a 1.26 ERA over 14.1 innings last October, including eight scoreless frames against the rival Red Sox in the Wild Card Round. He will now be asked to shoulder a heavier load.
It remains to be seen who the odd-man out would be in a series that calls for a three-man staff, though Rodón has made his case with a 1.42 ERA, 0.75 WHIP and 28 strikeouts in 25.1 innings in September.
1. Los Angeles Dodgers
12 of 12
RHP Yoshinobu Yamamoto (14-9, 2.53 ERA, 0.87 WHIP, 182 K, 185.0 IP)
LHP Tarik Skubal (4-2, 2.95 ERA, 1.13 WHIP, 60 K, 55.0 IP)
LHP Blake Snell (4-1, 1.86 ERA, 1.09 WHIP, 52 K, 38.2 IP)
RHP Tyler Glasnow (5-2, 3.53 ERA, 0.95 WHIP, 98 K, 74.0 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Emmet Sheehan, LHP Justin Wrobleski
The Dodgers have once again navigated much of the regular season without Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow, but they are healthy rolling into October and poised to round out the playoff rotation alongside Yoshinobu Yamamoto and deadline pickup Tarik Skubal.
The starting rotation logged a 2.68 ERA over 104 innings last postseason, with Yamamoto, Snell and Glasnow starting 13 of 17 games and the rest going to Shohei Ohtani, who will be limited to DH duties but has been sufficiently replaced by a two-time Cy Young winner in Skubal.
Right-hander Emmet Sheehan has a 0.53 ERA and 24 strikeouts over 17 innings in three September starts. He will serve as a multi-inning weapon out of the bullpen.

item.content:encoded:
With the Wild Card round of the 2026 MLB Playoffs behind us, it's time for the Division Series to get underway. It all starts on Saturday with all four Division Series matchups.
With that in mind, we polled the Rotoworld Baseball staff for their thoughts on how the rest of the postseason will play out. Check out our picks and analysis for the Division Series, Championship Series, and World Series.
The 2026 MLB postseason has arrived. Stay up to date with the latest results and more.
2026 ALDS, NLDS Predictions
| Writer | White Sox vs. Guardians | Yankees vs. Rays | Braves vs. Dodgers | Padres vs. Brewers |
| Eric Samulski | Guardians | Yankees | Dodgers | Brewers |
| Matthew Pouliot | Guardians | Yankees | Dodgers | Brewers |
| David Shovein | Guardians | Rays | Dodgers | Brewers |
| Christopher Crawford | White Sox | Yankees | Dodgers | Padres |
| D.J. Short | Guardians | Yankees | Dodgers | Padres |
White Sox vs. Guardians
Crawford: I don't think there's much of a difference between the White Sox and the Guardians. I think the fact that the White Sox already won a pair of postseason games on the road, both relatively convincingly, is something working in their favor. I can't quite go team of destiny or any of that stuff, but there does seem to be something about this White Sox team. I realize that's not exactly the most scientific answer, but my heart believes in the Chicago Popes.
Yankees vs. Rays
Short: The Rays and Yankees are set to meet in the postseason for the second time ever, and the first with actual fans in the building. While the Rays were the better regular season team this year, I think the Yankees are better built for the postseason. It starts with the rotation, which was the best in the majors with a 3.30 ERA, but their bullpen was even better with a 3.15 ERA. Drew Rasmussen has dominated the Yankees in his career, but New York has a level of rotation depth the Rays simply can't match.
Aaron Judge's status for the ALDS remains uncertain because of his calf injury, but even without him, one could argue that the Yankees have the more dangerous lineup. Their ability to change the game with one swing is something I think will win out over Tampa Bay's small-ball style in a short series.
Braves vs. Dodgers
Pouliot: Atlanta's pitching staff received 7 2/3 innings from Chris Sale and seven from Tyler Mahle and still seemed hard-pressed to get through the three-game Wild Card series against the Phillies. How are they going to hold up without those two to start the series against the Dodgers? Even without the relief appearance Thursday, starting Sale in Game 2 would have required pitching him on four days' rest, which he hasn't done since early April. As is, it looks like Sale in Game 3 and Mahle in Game 4. Maybe the Dodgers' bats start off cold and the Braves can steal a game in Los Angeles, but as shorthanded as they are in terms of pitching depth, not having their rotation lined puts them at a major disadvantage.
Padres vs. Brewers
Samulski: The Padres have been red hot and dominated the Cubs, but I published an article before the postseason with research from the last 10 years that showed teams coming into the playoffs with tons of momentum don't meaningfully perform better than teams who struggle coming into the postseason. I might as well trust my own research. The Brewers have been arguably the best team in baseball all season. Their lineup is incredibly tough to get out, and they have possibly the deepest overall pitching staff in the postseason.
Full MLB Postseason Predictions
| Writer | ALCS Winner | NLCS Winner | World Series Champion |
| Eric Samulski | New York Yankees | Milwaukee Brewers | Milwaukee Brewers |
| Matthew Pouliot | New York Yankees | Los Angeles Dodgers | Los Angeles Dodgers |
| David Shovein | Tampa Bay Rays | Milwaukee Brewers | Tampa Bay Rays |
| Christopher Crawford | New York Yankees | San Diego Padres | San Diego Padres |
| D.J. Short | New York Yankees | San Diego Padres | New York Yankees |
Samulski: I will admit my bias again when talking about why I picked against the Yankees. I just think this Brewers team is finally going to break through. The Yankees were lights out against the Red Sox, but they have been prone to strikeouts throughout the season. That can make them a volatile offense, and I think the consistency of the Brewers will win the day here.
Pouliot: A few weeks ago, I might have picked another champ, but with the Dodgers' bullpen rounding into form, their biggest potential weakness seems gone. Edwin Díaz still isn't a sure thing, but he was much improved after coming off the IL, allowing just one hit and one walk while striking out nine in his final five innings. Roki Sasaki and Evan Phillips both hit 100 mph last week, and Kris Bubic, if he's even needed, could prove to be a secret weapon. Shohei Ohtani and Freddie Freeman might not be able to carry the offense at this point, but even if the Dodgers are lacking their usual firepower, they should be able to win some low-scoring games.
Crawford: I don't think the Padres are the best team in baseball. I don't think they're even the best team in their division. But I love the way they're playing now, and that bullpen, quality starters at the top of the rotation and just enough star power makes me believe they're built for the postseason, and their first-ever World Series championship.
Short: I love the Yankees' pitching and Aaron Judge should be back eventually in some capacity, which only improves the team's outlook for a potential World Series matchup. As opposed to their meeting in 1998, I would expect the Padres to make this one much more competitive. San Diego's offense has been great in the second half and their bullpen is positively scary. Still, the Yankees would hold the major edge in starting pitching, and that would ultimately make the difference in my hypothetical World Series matchup.

item.content:encoded:
After a thorough dismantling of the Red Sox in a Wild Card sweep, the Yankees are riding high. Their offense torched Boston's pitchers, scoring 18 runs on 26 hits and swatting four homers in the two-game set. Next up is another division rival, the 98-win Tampa Bay Rays.
Tampa's starting rotation finished second in the AL to the Yankees in ERA, though they did so in 56 fewer innings and with 176 fewer strikeouts. They're expected to hand the ball to the perennially-underrated Drew Rasmussen in Game 1. The 31-year-old has posted a sub-3.00 ERA in each of his six seasons with Tampa, though a couple of those have been severely shortened by injury. He made 30 starts this year and tossed a career-high 172 innings, going 16-5 with a 2.67 ERA while leading the league in WHIP (0.913) and K:BB ratio (5.44). He finished the season particularly strong, allowing six runs over his last six starts. Of note, he threw a career-high 114 pitches in his last outing of the season, hinting that Kevin Cash, the notoriously short-leashed Rays skipper, may be looking for his ace to shoulder a larger burden than usual.
Like Cam Schlittler, Rasmussen's top three pitches are all fastballs: a cutter, a four-seamer, and a sinker. All three have been lights-out; opponents hit .205 and slugged .326 against the cutter this season, the best they fared against any of the three. He mixes in a changeup that he threw 354 times without allowing an extra-base hit and, less frequently, a curveball and a sweeper. The only item missing from the two-time All-Star's portfolio is postseason excellence — he's made just one playoff start, back in 2021, in which he allowed three runs in two innings before getting the hook.
Cash has remained noncommittal on how he'll deploy the rest of his pitching staff. Freddy Peralta, Nick Martinez, Griffin Jax, and Ian Seymour were Rasmussen's rotation-mates and all are expected to feature in some capacity. After a nightmare first half with the Mets, Peralta rebounded nicely with the Rays. The right-hander went 5-0 with a microscopic 0.79 ERA over his last six starts of the year, earning AL Pitcher of the Month honors for September while regaining the form that saw him finish fifth in NL Cy Young voting last year and firmly entrenching himself in the playoff picture.
Martinez was one of the best value signings of the offseason, winning 15 games along with a 3.10 ERA on a one-year, $9 million deal. The 36-year-old faded a bit down the stretch, allowing 20 runs in 42 innings across his last eight starts, and it's fair to wonder if his career-high 180 innings have caught up with him. The Rays converted Jax from a reliever to a starter midseason and the results were strong. He had a lower ERA in the rotation (3.14) than in the bullpen (8.00) but threw 75 pitches or more in just six of his 23 starts. None of those came in his five September appearances, meaning he'd likely be used more as a bulk arm than a true starter if he does get an October start. Seymour also began the year in the bullpen, though he topped 90 pitches six times after moving to the rotation. He's the only southpaw of the bunch, a fact which could either make him an attracting starting option or a valuable multi-inning reliever against a Yankees lineup featuring a bevy of lefties. So, too, does the fact that he faced the Bombers in his final start of the season and shoved, holding them to one baserunner in five scoreless innings.
With the addition of a superfluous starter or two, the Rays' bullpen will be a deep, veteran group. Bryan Baker is the team's shutdown closer, posting a 1.44 ERA that trailed only Toronto's Louis Varland among qualified relievers while tying for the MLB lead with 41 saves. His .203 BABIP is an outlier, though, suggesting some confluence of good luck and playing into a defense that graded out as the best in the AL by DRS. The last time Baker blew a save was back on May 13th. He relies primarily on a four-seamer against which opponents hit .125 with no home runs this season and a changeup that sits more than 10 mph lower.
Cash's top setup option is Kevin Kelly, who appeared in a club-high 71 games. Kelly pitched to a 2.44 ERA on the season but struggled down the stretch, allowing seven runs in his last eight innings of work. Behind those two, the pecking order is less clear. Cam Booser has been the most effective lefty in the 'pen, recording a sub-2.00 ERA in 41 innings. Fellow southpaws Garrett Cleavinger and Steven Matz had down years after strong 2025s, as did right-hander Cole Sulser. Casey Legumina is another righty option, as is Tyler Wells, who allowed three earned runs in 18 innings after coming over from Baltimore at the trade deadline.
Wells and Cleavinger ended the season on the IL with forearm tightness but each pitched an inning in a scrimmage Tuesday and could be in play. Tampa's bullpen ERA of 3.99 is more middle-of-the-pack than the performance of its starters, but they still have clear lanes to get through the late innings.
In looking at the Rays' pitching corps as a whole, Rasmussen looms large as their greatest differentiator. He's a tough matchup for any team, but if the Yankees can get to him tonight with their third starter on the hill, they'll do a great deal to puncture the Rays' confidence and derail their winning formula. After Game 1, the Yankees will likely need to contend with a kitchen sink approach from Cash, who can be expected to make aggressive, matchup-based moves to put his pitchers in positions to succeed.

item.title: [Chicago Tribune] Column: Can the Chicago White Sox keep succeeding in the postseason without a conventional rotation?
item.dc:creator: Paul Sullivan

item.content:encoded:
CLEVELAND — If you’re a baseball fan of a certain age, you’ve probably spent most of your life knowing some certainties about a pitching staff.
The five best guys (or four if you’re really old) are the starters who will try to get you through the bulk of the game. The best reliever is the closer, who pitches the last inning or possibly part of the eighth if he’s dominant enough. The next-best relievers — preferably one left-hander and one right-hander — are the setup men, the potential bridges from starter to closer.
And the pitcher who is least effective on the staff is the mop-up man, whose main function is keeping the better relievers from being overused.
For years managers used that basic blueprint, or something close to it, to get through the regular season. Then when the playoffs arrived, the best three or four starters went longer because the season was almost over and they could empty their bullets in the biggest games.
But baseball has changed, for better or worse, and now anything goes. Boston Red Sox ace Sonny Gray was removed in the fifth inning of a do-or-die wild-card game Wednesday, and Gray and his teammates grumbled about how the game got to this point.
Which brings us to the 2026 Chicago White Sox, who are trying to win with a “no-rotation” rotation.
Will Venable, the second-year White Sox manager, announced Friday that left-handed reliever Hagen Smith would start Game 1 of the American League Division Series against the Cleveland Guardians, serving as the opener Saturday, as he did in pitching three scoreless innings in Game 1 of the wild-card win in Houston.
It’s no surprise. The Sox have used openers a league-leading 32 times this season, including Smith’s outing Tuesday. If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it.
But does the no-rotation rotation have its limits, or can Venable’s Sox keep succeeding in the postseason with a bullpen-first strategy?
Venable acknowledged Sean Burke could start Game 2 on Monday, as he did in a four-inning start in Game 2 against the Astros, in which starters Anthony Kay and Erick Fedde both pitched in relief. But other than Burke, it might be a guessing game from here on out.
Can Smith come back to start Game 3 at home Wednesday, giving him three starts in their first five playoff games? Who knows what’s up Venable’s sleeve?
“I think the way it’s set up with these off days, we’re going to leverage the arms that we want to leverage when we want to use them throughout these first couple,” Venable said. “And if that means that one of the guys who we’ve been giving starts to throughout the season takes a bulk role in that, there’s certainly potential for that. But I think you can expect us to mix and match and use our best arms in the most optimal way.”
That suggests Smith and Grant Taylor can be the designated bookends of multiple games, with Jordan Hicks, David Sandlin and Sean Newcomb in the middle and Kay, Fedde and Davis Martin as the wild cards.
It’s almost the polar-opposite approach that then-manager Ozzie Guillén employed in the 2005 postseason, when José Contreras, Mark Buehrle, Freddy Garcia and Jon Garland combined for a 2.84 ERA in 12 starts, leading the Sox on an 11-1 run to their World Series title.
In the five-game win over the Anaheim Angels in the AL Championship Series, the four starters had four straight complete games and combined for 44 1/3 of the 45 total innings, with Neal Cotts contributing the other two outs in the ninth inning of the Game 1 loss. The rest of the bullpen had a nice seat to watch the starters dealing.
“I don’t know if you’ll ever see that again,” Sox catcher A.J. Pierzynski said afterward. “Managers just don’t do that anymore. They don’t have confidence to let guys go 120 pitches and throw nine innings.”
In the World Series, advance scout Bryan Little and his crew gave Guillén and pitching coach Don Cooper a near-perfect report on strengths and weaknesses of the Astros hitters. Contreras and Buerhle both went seven innings in the first two wins at Sox Park, and Garland went seven in Game 3 in Houston before the Astros tied it off Dustin Hermanson in the eighth.
Guillén was forced to use his well-rested bullpen when the game went 14 innings but also used Orlando “El Duque” Hernández and Buehrle. After Geoff Blum’s go-ahead home run in the 14th, Buehrle notched the infamous “buzzed save” by getting the final out after having a few beers in the clubhouse. “No more than three … I swear,” he later said.
Buehrle wound up on a Wheaties box, but he didn’t become a legend for his cereal-eating habits.
Game 4 was as old-school as it gets, with Garcia going seven shutout innings, Cliff Politte and Cotts getting the Sox through the eighth and Bobby Jenks closing out a 1-0 win to start the parade plans.
“That type of game is like the ones I watched for 162 games during the regular season,” Guillén said in the celebratory clubhouse.
Venable’s approach in the postseason also mirrors what he has done for much of the season.
General manager Chris Getz knew he didn’t have a dominant rotation in spring training, and opening-day starter Shane Smith was quickly dispatched to Triple-A Charlotte after three starts. Martin, Burke, Kay and Fedde have been the mainstays, though Fedde, who signed at the start of spring training, had only 15 starts in his 33 games.
Taylor has evolved into the de facto closer but can go three innings if needed. He also was used as an opener in April. Seranthony Domínguez led the team 12 saves, even after being dispatched at the trade deadline.
Openers aren’t a new concept. “Bullpenning” has been around for the last decade. Cubs manager Craig Counsell also used openers in last year’s postseason.
But is it possible no team has been as unconventional as the ’26 Sox in this particular run?
“It’s possible,” Getz said during the wild-card celebration. “We weren’t trying to re-create the wheel. We were trying to optimize the group that we had. So much of (baseball) has relied on starting pitching. We would’ve liked to do that. But if we were trying to win games, we had to lean on the strength of the club, and we’ve done that.”
The Sox’s strategy has been criticized, especially when an opener puts the bulk pitcher in a hole. Guillén himself has said on the Chicago Sports Network he’s not a fan of openers.
But if the Sox go all the way without a true rotation, the players may never have to buy a meal or drink in Chicago again. Or at least that’s the adage.
“More often than not I’ll just roll in and buy a drink or buy my dinner,” Blum told me last week in Houston. “But every so often, if there is a hard-core Sox fan in the bar or in the restaurant, there will be a free drink that will show up once in a while.”
So it’s kind of true?
“It still carries a little bit of weight,” Blum said. “We’re not quite the ’85 Bears, but the ’05 Sox do OK.”

item.content:encoded:
Why Royals' Vinnie Pasquantino believes White Sox are 'built' for playoffs appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
Vinnie Pasquantino has spent enough time facing the Chicago White Sox to know their bullpen presents a tougher task than the name recognition might suggest. That experience has the Kansas City Royals first baseman believing Chicago can push the Cleveland Guardians to the limit in the ALDS.
The White Sox head into Saturday afternoon's opener after sweeping the Houston Astros in the Wild Card round. Pasquantino sees a pitching staff capable of helping them extend that postseason run.
"In my opinion, the White Sox are built for these series because they can just go to the bullpen," Pasquantino said on The Rich Eisen Show. "If you look at some of the names in the bullpen, as a casual fan or if you don't know the White Sox, you don't think much of it. But having faced these guys, it is uncomfortable at-bats; their pitching coach does a great job…"
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
"I do think the White Sox are alive in this series for sure."
—@VPasquantino on the White Sox ahead of their series against the Guardians ⚾️
(via @RichEisenShow) pic.twitter.com/RMXt0MCWmC
— SportsCenter (@SportsCenter) October 2, 2026
That assessment carries weight coming from a division opponent. Pasquantino's confidence comes from standing in the batter's box against those pitchers, where unfamiliar names can quickly become difficult matchups.
A reliable bullpen also gives Chicago flexibility in a short series. The White Sox can turn to relief options when a starter struggles or a matchup calls for a change, rather than waiting for an inning to get away from them.
But Pasquantino identified a complication: Cleveland knows those arms, too.
"The disadvantage is that they are playing a team they have played all year. If anyone is going to know the White Sox, it's the Guardians," he said. "I think this series will go five. Whoever plays the little things better will win that series. I do think the White Sox are alive in this series for sure."
The regular-season results support his expectation of a close matchup. Chicago edged Cleveland 7-6, with only a one-run differential between the teams.
Related: White Sox reveal who will pitch against Guardians' Parker Messick in ALDS Game 1

item.description: The season for the Houston Astros came to an unceremonious close at the hands of the Chicago White Sox, who beat them two games to none in the MLB Wild Card Playoff round. Now, the White Sox move on to face the divisional rival Cleveland Guardians in the Divisional Playoff round, while the Astros are left picking up the pieces and wondering where things went wrong. item.content:encoded:
The season for the Houston Astros came to an unceremonious close at the hands of the Chicago White Sox, who beat them two games to none in the MLB Wild Card Playoff round.
Now, the White Sox move on to face the divisional rival Cleveland Guardians in the Divisional Playoff round, while the Astros are left picking up the pieces and wondering where things went wrong.
Not long afterward, starter Hunter Brown expressed his frustration with how things turned out in a completely blunt recap.
Houston Astros Pitcher Hunter Brown Admits The Tough Truth After Series Loss To White Sox
Brown's start in Game 2 against the White Sox ended before the first inning was over, forcing the Astros to turn to their bullpen early. The Astros had already utilized eight pitchers during their Game 1 setback, and they also used six more in their regular season finale.
Brown faced nine Chicago batters, allowing five hits and four runs, three of which were earned. He also walked one batter and while also not getting much help from his teammates. The Astros committed a pair of costly errors, while Yordan Alvarez failed to catch a playable fly ball.
Ultimately, the White Sox picked up a 7-3 win, sweeping the Astros out of the playoffs and ending their dreams of another World Series run.
Afterward, Brown said that his performance wasn't up to snuff despite his best efforts.
"I feel like everything that could have went poorly did and I didn't overcome the whole inning, really," Brown said, per Brian McTaggart of MLB.com. "I felt like, looking back, it's hard to say I don't take anything back, but I feel like pitches that I threw I was confident and I threw them to the best of my ability. Just didn't come out on the right end of it. Unfortunately, that's the way it went, and they were able to slap a crooked number up there on the board."
A shoulder strain limited Brown's availability during the 2026 regular season, which saw him finish with a 3.19 ERA in 20 starts.
Hunter Brown Has Played His Entire MLB Career With The Astros
Brown was taken by the Astros in the fifth round (166th overall pick) of the 2019 MLB Draft. After making his professional debut that year, he missed the entire 2020 minor league season before moving through Double-A and Triple-A in 2021.
Brown broke out in 2022 with Triple-A Sugar Land, posting a 2.55 ERA and 106 innings while earning PCL Pitcher of the Year honors. His performance also made him Houston's top prospect and one of MLB's most highly regarded young pitchers.
Brown helped Houston win the 2022 World Series before becoming a full-time starter in 2023. After a strong second half in 2024, he broke out in 2025 with a 2.43 ERA, 206 strikeouts and his first All-Star selection.
This article was originally published on HEAVY

item.content:encoded:
October 02, 2026
Ryan Howard twisted uncomfortably out of the batter's box, then crumpled just a few steps down the first-base line as the St. Louis Cardinals rushed toward the mound to celebrate.
An October-fueled Citizens Bank Park fell silent.
The Phillies had lost Game 5 of the 2011 NLDS, and suddenly, shockingly, their all-in chase after another World Series title was over.
Roy Halladay, with his last bit of true greatness, tossed a one-run gem that should've been enough of a chance, and yet was nullified by an even more brilliant complete game from Chris Carpenter, who made a Philadelphia lineup flush with high-profile bats look entirely pedestrian.
And then there was Howard at the end, the star slugger who was left lying there in the grass as the Phillies' grand ambitions all came crashing down.
No one wanted to say it out loud at the time. Maybe they just couldn't bring themselves to fully accept it just yet. But that image has since been permanently etched into the minds of every Phillies fan who witnessed it, because deep down, everyone knew right then and there: A golden era of Phillies baseball was over.
One by one, the generation defined by Howard, Jimmy Rollins, Chase Utley, Cole Hamels, that second-ever World Championship in 2008, and then Halladay, Cliff Lee, and any other big name that the organization could get its hands on in the pursuit of one more, faded.
Those Phillies were never competitive again.
Bryce Harper whiffed on a low and way, way away slider from Chris Sale that he never had a prayer of hitting, and that Drake Baldwin, behind the plate, never had a prayer of catching.
Harper, slowly and totally unaware, bent down to take his shin guard off, thinking it was strike three and that the inning was over. He never saw the ball spike past Baldwin in the dirt, and go rolling to the backstop. By the time he realized, all he gave was a disinterested jog up the first base line, which did finally end the eighth inning from Baldwin having the time to recover for the throw up to the base.
John Kruk: "RUN!"
Bryce Harper was slow to get out of the box, not realizing strike three had gotten away.
(Via: @MLB) pic.twitter.com/GRcx3VGWtQ
— Foul Territory (@FoulTerritoryTV) October 2, 2026
The Phillies were down, 6-2, in the deciding Game 3 of the 2026 NL Wild Card series, on the road against the rival Atlanta Braves.
They still had three outs of life left, but everyone watching knew full well – and probably had no hesitation admitting this time, just shy of 15 years later – that another playoff era of Phillies baseball was over.
And once this club does get back to South Philadelphia, there will be no World Series pennant to look up at in center field and over Ashburn Alley.
The closest this generation ever got was that first breakout run that burnt out against the Astros in 2022.
They only ever got further away from it from there, and now might be all out of chances.
The Phillies stood in the visiting clubhouse, and interim manager Don Mattingly sat at the press conference dais.
No one spoke with any certainties.
Mattingly, who took over midseason for Rob Thomson, talked around whether he wanted to come back and how he felt about the decision the Phillies will have to make this winter for whoever their next full-time manager is going to be.
"It's not the time to talk about anything like that," Mattingly said. "...I want the Phillies to do what they need to do."
Granted, anything shy of a World Series always seemed to point toward him not staying.
Alec Bohm, the first-round and homegrown infielder who was good but always had better expected of him, is now headed for free agency and didn't want to talk about what his future held either.
Trea Turner, who certainly will be back just by the nature of his enormous 11-year, $300 million contract, knows he can't with another season like this one, where his numbers at the plate are low and where you can never be fully confident that he'll properly field the baseball. That can't cut it.
"[I] got a lot of work to do," Turner said.
And then there was Harper, who didn't have much to offer either, save for one definitive statement.
"I'd imagine this team's gonna look a lot different next year," said Harper, "with the guys that are kind of leaving this clubhouse. We'll see."
If there even is a next year for baseball.
Either way, it does feel like this team has to be.
The next few weeks are undoubtedly going to put the Phillies and everyone responsible for their current construction up to harsh scrutiny, amid a fan base that, really, got tired of them two postseason failures ago.
Dave Dombrowski, the Phillies' president of baseball operations, will have the most to answer for, after he repeatedly ran it back with an aging core, failed once again to put together a competent bullpen, and ended this season with none of his trade deadline acquisitions on the postseason roster, all while presiding over a barren-looking farm system.
Hitting coach Kevin Long, who has long been immune from any other shifts in the dugout staff around him, has to face the music here, too, after the Phillies continued to have a collectively abysmal approach at the plate – outside of a month – and after seeing nearly all of the Phils' batters either plateau, regress, or in the case of Luis Arráez, to see a perennial .300-plus hitter suddenly drop well below that line the second he put on a red-pinstriped uniform.
And then there's Harper, the big face of an era that kept falling short and now might not even be good enough to get there to begin with anymore.
All offseason and into spring training, it was clear he was miffed by Dombrowski openly questioning to the press last fall whether he could be "elite" anymore.
Harper said back in February that it wasn't something to motivate him, but he made it obvious, too, that those remarks stuck in his craw.
And he would go on to put up solid numbers, and yeah, he even had his heroics in a Game 2 that kept the Phillies alive for another day.
But now they're done. This era might be done, and with its end forever tied to that moment of Harper leisurely taking his shin guard off at the plate, not knowing the ball went rolling, and by the time he did, not having enough care to even try to fully run it out.
It felt a lot like Ryan Howard 15 years ago. It felt like an era was over.
This one, though, might be a bit more bitter.
*QUOTES SOURCE: NBC Sports Philadelphia on YouTube
Follow Nick on Twitter: @itssnick
Follow Nick on Bluesky: @itssnick
Like us on Facebook: PhillyVoice Sports

item.title: [MLB.com] Here's how the pitching might line up for the White Sox-Guardians ALDS
item.dc:creator: Tim Stebbins; Scott Merkin
item.description: CLEVELAND -- While battling for the American League Central title last month, the Guardians and White Sox divisional race featured an added reward: a first-round bye in the postseason that would allow the champ to set its preferred pitching plan for the AL Division Series. That’s where we find ourselves now, as Cleveland and Chicago get set for their first-ever playoff matchup.
